What is Open Access?

Open Access is an initiative that aims to make scientific research freely available to all. To date our community has made over 100 million downloads. It’s based on principles of collaboration, unobstructed discovery, and, most importantly, scientific progression. As PhD students, we found it difficult to access the research we needed, so we decided to create a new Open Access publisher that levels the playing field for scientists across the world. How? By making research easy to access, and puts the academic needs of the researchers before the business interests of publishers.

Authors, Editors and Institutions

We are a community of more than 103,000 authors and editors from 3,291 institutions spanning 160 countries, including Nobel Prize winners and some of the world’s most-cited researchers. Publishing on IntechOpen allows authors to earn citations and find new collaborators, meaning more people see your work not only from your own field of study, but from other related fields too.

1. Introduction

Mycotoxins are naturally occurring toxic compounds produced by certain molds. They may be found in food and feed when susceptible raw materials are affected by fungi before harvest, after harvest, during transport, or during storage. Their relevance to food safety is not limited to visible mold growth. A commodity may appear acceptable and still contain toxin levels that require control, while contamination within a lot may be uneven. This creates a practical challenge for sampling, testing, risk evaluation, and decision-making.

The main fungal genera linked with mycotoxin formation include Aspergillus, Fusarium, Penicillium, and Claviceps. Several hundred mycotoxins have been identified, although food safety work most often focuses on groups such as, aflatoxins, ochratoxin A, patulin, fumonisins, zearalenone, deoxynivalenol, nivalenol, T-2 and HT-2 toxins, and ergot alkaloids [1, 2]. These compounds differ in their chemical properties, toxic effects, occurrence patterns, and commodity associations. For this reason, the term “mycotoxins” should not be treated as a single, uniform hazard. It refers to a broad group of fungal metabolites that require separate toxicological evaluation and commodity-specific control measures.

Mycotoxin contamination is shaped by the interaction among crop biology, weather, fungal ecology, insect damage, agronomic practices, harvest timing, drying, storage, processing, trade, and consumer habits. Warm and humid conditions often favor fungal growth, but each toxin–crop combination has its own set of conditions. Cereals, nuts, dried fruits, spices, apples, coffee beans, oilseeds, and animal feeds are among the product categories commonly discussed in relation to these contaminants [3]. Because many affected commodities are traded internationally, a local contamination event may become a wider food and feed safety matter.

2. Food and feed chains as routes of exposure

Human exposure may occur directly through contaminated plant-based foods or indirectly through foods of animal origin when animals consume contaminated feed. A well-known example is the conversion of aflatoxin B1 from feed into aflatoxin M1 in milk [4]. This route is of particular interest in dairy safety because milk and dairy products are widely consumed, including by infants and young children. Control of mycotoxins in animal feed is therefore a part of food safety control, not only animal production management.

The health effects associated with mycotoxins vary by compound, dose, duration of exposure, nutritional status, age, and coexisting health conditions. Acute exposure to high levels may cause rapid illness, while long-term low-level exposure is often more difficult to assess because it depends on dietary patterns and repeated intake [5]. Aflatoxins receive close attention because naturally occurring aflatoxins have been classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer as carcinogenic to humans, and aflatoxins are also described by EFSA as genotoxic and carcinogenic [6, 7]. Other mycotoxins are linked with effects on the kidney, liver, immune function, gastrointestinal tract, reproduction, or endocrine activity, depending on the compound and the evidence available [5]. In agriculture, mycotoxins are linked with plant health, crop stress, fungal infection, drying, and storage. In veterinary medicine, they may affect animal performance, feed intake, reproduction, or immunity. In analytical chemistry, mycotoxins require validated sampling plans and methods that can deal with low concentrations and uneven distribution. In public health, they require exposure assessment across dietary groups. In regulation, they require maximum levels, monitoring programs, official controls, and risk communication. This amplitude explains why the field is best approached through collaboration among agronomists, microbiologists, toxicologists, veterinarians, food technologists, laboratory specialists, regulators, and food business operators.

3. Stability, processing, and the limits of end-product control

One of the practical difficulties in mycotoxin management is that many mycotoxins are chemically stable. The World Health Organization notes that most mycotoxins survive food processing, and the FAO states that they can remain after common operations such as, milling, baking, boiling, roasting, or juicing [8, 9]. Processing may reduce some toxin levels in certain cases, for example, through sorting, cleaning, dehulling, removal of visibly damaged material, or dilution through compliant raw materials. However, processing should not be treated as a full corrective measure for contaminated lots.

This is why prevention has priority over late-stage correction. Good agricultural practices, crop rotation, pest control, establishing the optimal harvest time, rapid drying, water activity control, clean storage spaces, separation of suspect batches, traceability, and routine testing contribute to reducing exposure to mycotoxins. The preventive approach must begin before raw materials enter a factory or feed mill. Once contamination is established, the available options may become limited, costly, and subject to legal restrictions.

Sampling is another important element, as mycotoxins can occur in “hot spots,” where a small part of a batch contains higher levels than the rest. Thus, batch definition, sample size, sample preparation, grinding, homogenization, selection of analytical method, recovery, measurement uncertainty, and interpretation in relation to legal limits are all relevant to the final control decision. A result cannot be interpreted correctly without knowing how the sample was taken and prepared.

4. Regulation and risk-based control

International and regional regulatory systems treat mycotoxins as contaminants of food and feed requiring risk-based control. At the global level, the Codex Alimentarius Commission sets maximum levels and codes of practice for certain contaminants and natural toxins, based on scientific risk assessments carried out by the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives [10]. At the European level, maximum levels for certain contaminants in food are set in Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 [11]. EFSA also supports risk managers by evaluating data on occurrence, exposure, toxicology, and transfer from feed to food of animal origin. Legal limits are necessary, but they do not replace preventive management. They define acceptability at specified points in the chain, while good practices and monitoring reduce the probability that noncompliant batches will occur. A risk-based control system should therefore combine supplier approval, raw material specifications, seasonal risk evaluation, analytical surveillance, storage controls, corrective actions, and review of trend data. For commodities with known vulnerability, testing frequency should reflect origin, crop year, weather conditions, supplier history, processing use, and intended consumer group.

The effect of climate change adds further pressure to this approach. The European Environment Agency reported in 2025 that climate change could alter fungal behavior and distribution, increasing the risk of exposure to some mycotoxins [12]. Changes in temperature, rainfall, drought, insect pressure, and crop patterns may alter the occurrence of fungal infection and toxin formation. The food and feed sectors, therefore, need surveillance systems that can respond to changing raw material risks rather than relying only on historic patterns.

5. Conclusions

Mycotoxins remain a demanding subject for food and feed safety because they sit at the junction of natural contamination, agricultural practice, animal production, food processing, laboratory control, toxicology, and regulation. Their control depends on early prevention, sound sampling, reliable analysis, clear legal interpretation, and decisions based on risk.

An interdisciplinary view is, therefore, a practical requirement. Farmers, feed manufacturers, food businesses, laboratories, health authorities, and regulators each hold part of the control chain. Thus, mycotoxin management should be seen as a continuous process that starts with crop health and ends only when safe food reaches the consumer (European Food Safety Authority).
